\section[el aduanero]{el aduanero — the customs officer}

\label{lesson:ES-C656-aduanero}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to feel sick, then the Spanish for the waistcoat.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el aduanero}
\textbf{el aduanero} — \textquotedblleft{}the customs officer\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
El aduanero abre mi maleta.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The customs officer opens my suitcase.}
\end{quote}

A woman is \emph{la aduanera}. As an adjective: \emph{el control aduanero}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{aduanero} is built on \emph{aduana} \textquotedblleft{}customs\textquotedblright{}, which comes from Andalusian Arabic \emph{ad-dīwān} \textquotedblleft{}the office\textquotedblright{}, Arabic \emph{dīwān} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el aduanero}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el aduanero}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{el aduanero}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to feel sick, then the Spanish for the waistcoat, then say \emph{el aduanero} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[la aduana]{la aduana — customs}

\label{lesson:ES-C656-aduana}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the waistcoat, then the Spanish for the customs officer.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la aduana}
\textbf{la aduana} — \textquotedblleft{}customs\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
En la aduana revisan las maletas.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{At customs they check the suitcases.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Pasar la aduana} — to go through customs.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{aduana} comes from Andalusian Arabic \emph{ad-dīwān} \textquotedblleft{}the office\textquotedblright{}, from Arabic \emph{dīwān} \textquotedblleft{}administrative office, register\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la aduana}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la aduana}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the waistcoat, then the Spanish for the customs officer, then say \emph{la aduana} again

\section[el visado]{el visado — the visa}

\label{lesson:ES-C656-visado}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the customs officer, then the Spanish for customs.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el visado}
\textbf{el visado} — \textquotedblleft{}the visa\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Para este país necesitas visado.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{You need a visa for this country.}
\end{quote}

Spain says \emph{el visado}; Latin America says \emph{la visa}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{visado} is built on \emph{visar} \textquotedblleft{}to endorse, to stamp as seen\textquotedblright{}, which is usually linked to \emph{visa}; Spanish \emph{visa} was borrowed from French \emph{visa}, from Latin \emph{vīsa} \textquotedblleft{}things seen\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), built on \emph{vidēre} \textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el visado}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el visado}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{el visado}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the customs officer, then the Spanish for customs, then say \emph{el visado} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[sellar]{sellar — to stamp; to seal}

\label{lesson:ES-C656-sellar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for customs, then the Spanish for the visa.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: sellar}
\textbf{sellar} — \textquotedblleft{}to stamp; to seal\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
En la frontera me sellaron el pasaporte.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{They stamped my passport at the border.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Sellar un sobre} — to seal an envelope.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{sellar} is inherited from Vulgar Latin \emph{sigellāre}, Latin \emph{sigillāre} \textquotedblleft{}to seal\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from \emph{sigillum} \textquotedblleft{}a seal\textquotedblright{}, a little \emph{signum} \textquotedblleft{}sign\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[registrar]{registrar — to search; to register, to record}

\label{lesson:ES-C656-registrar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the visa, then the Spanish for to stamp.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: registrar}
\textbf{registrar} — \textquotedblleft{}to search; to register, to record\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
La policía registró el coche.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The police searched the car.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Registrarse} is to check in or sign up: \emph{registrarse en el hotel}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{registrar} is built on \emph{registro} \textquotedblleft{}register\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), which comes from Medieval Latin \emph{registrum}, from \emph{regesta} \textquotedblleft{}things recorded\textquotedblright{}, built on \emph{gerere} \textquotedblleft{}to carry, to carry out\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the visa, then the Spanish for to stamp, then say \emph{registrar} again
